The numerical inputs are \path{data/load_profiles.csv} and \path{data/shiftability_profile.csv}, whose active slots 1--96 are reproduced jointly in Table~\ref{tab:workload-inputs}. The load file also contains legacy rows 97--108; annual timeline construction does not use those rows. The former file specifies flexible and inflexible arrival utilisation at quarter-hour resolution. The main paper's workload table retains hourly means of these inputs: for example, flexible utilisation at 00:00, 00:15, 00:30 and 00:45 is 0.40, 0.38, 0.36 and 0.34, so its hourly mean is 0.37 rather than the hourly starting value of 0.40. The four individual values are used by the model. The contextual literature-range columns do not replace these exact inputs.

The tranche-share file is constructed from the 24 hourly distributions in the main paper's tranche table. Each hourly row is repeated four consecutive times: the 00:00 distribution applies at 00:00, 00:15, 00:30 and 00:45, followed by four copies of the 01:00 distribution, and so on. This gives 96 quarter-hour rows, each summing to one. The whole 24-row sequence is not repeated four times across the day. Table~\ref{tab:workload-inputs} and the supplied CSV reproduce the intended expansion exactly.

\section{Numerical checks and solution quality}
The retained manuscript run record identifies Python 3.12.0, Pyomo 6.10.1 and HiGHS 1.15.1, on Windows 11 with an eight-core AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D. Annual scenarios request a relative MILP gap of 0.1\%, with a standard daily time limit of 300 s and a normal acceptance threshold of 1\%. Feasible exceptions in sensitivity cases are disclosed below rather than treating every solve as proven optimal. The main paper's 5.050\% is computed from the retained annual settlements, not by summing daily objective bounds.

All fourteen annual summaries contain 365 local dates and 35,040 committed intervals. Their stored checks cover timestamp continuity, physical state handoff, workload conservation, storage mode exclusivity and signed-price settlement reconciliation. The stated audit tolerances are $10^{-5}$ in the native state units, $10^{-3}$ kW for power flows and $10^{-7}$ CPU-hours for work. Central operation also stores a cohort execution trace. The two central time-limited daily solutions, on 25 May and 4 October, have reported relative gaps of approximately 0.605\% and 0.385\%, within the normal threshold.

Table~\ref{tab:solver-quality} records the maximum original reported gap for each retained annual chain, including values above the normal threshold. Existing 900 s exact-state reruns of selected 25 May horizons provide additional evidence: the 0.75 UPS and TES cases achieve gaps of 0.627\% and 0.959\%; the 0.75 and 1.25 workload cases retain gaps of 1.015\% and 2.032\%. Across these intermediate checks, the largest committed-day cost change is GBP~0.281, with unchanged closing workload and physical-state differences no greater than $2.14\times10^{-14}$. The 0.5 workload case retains a 5.652\% gap in its existing 900 s check, but its reported absolute primal-bound width is GBP~0.102 and committed cost changes by approximately GBP~0.002. Near-zero negative objectives can produce large relative gaps despite small absolute bounds.

These reruns are diagnostics of particular horizons, not new full-year scenarios substituted into the table. Their limited effects support the displayed result precision in those checks; they do not prove a full-year global optimum or retrospectively certify every recorded exception. Original and diagnostic gap values must not be mixed into a single claim that all annual solves meet 1\%.

The existing year-end assessment confirms service of the 0.642875 CPU-hours outstanding at midnight. Its complete final look-ahead contains 2,313.104 kWh and GBP~89.542, including ordinary January demand. Existing terminal-value tests, using median-to-maximum observed 1 January prices with conversion adjustments, change annual cost by at most 0.000381\% in the tested earlier central chain. That report predates the cohort-trace central result and quotes a 5.049\% saving. It is supporting evidence for the terminal convention, not a replacement for the current 5.050\% result or a separate terminal-sensitivity proof for every capacity case.

For the event study, the retained summary records 288 cells, of which 275 carry the boundary/cap flag and thirteen an unresolved-next-step flag. \section{Numerical checks and solution quality}
The retained manuscript run record identifies Python 3.12.0, Pyomo 6.10.1 and HiGHS 1.15.1, on Windows 11 with an eight-core AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D. Annual scenarios request a relative MILP gap of 0.1\%, with a standard daily time limit of 300 s and a normal acceptance threshold of 1\%. Feasible exceptions in sensitivity cases are disclosed below rather than treating every solve as proven optimal. The main paper's 5.382\% is computed from the retained annual settlements, not by summing daily objective bounds.

All fourteen annual summaries contain 365 local dates and 35,040 committed intervals. Their stored checks cover timestamp continuity, physical state handoff, workload conservation, storage mode exclusivity and signed-price settlement reconciliation. The stated audit tolerances are $10^{-5}$ in the native state units, $10^{-3}$ kW for power flows and $10^{-7}$ CPU-hours for work. Central operation also stores a cohort execution trace. The three central time-limited daily solutions, on 25 May, 6 August and 4 October, have reported relative gaps of approximately 0.868\%, 0.228\% and 0.612\%, respectively, within the normal threshold.

\input{tables/solver_quality.tex}

Table~\ref{tab:solver-quality} records the maximum reported gap for each retained annual chain. Three 25 May sensitivity horizons exceed the normal 1\% threshold: the 0.5 workload, 0.5 UPS and 0.5 TES cases have gaps of 1.301\%, 1.111\% and 1.009\%, respectively. Their absolute daily objective-bound widths are GBP~0.103, 0.329 and 0.359. These feasible time-limited incumbents remain in the annual settlements and are disclosed as exceptions. Near-zero negative objectives can produce relative gaps above the threshold despite small absolute bounds. The accompanying \path{data/corrected_solver_horizons.csv} records every non-optimal termination in the corrected annual chains.

The daily bounds apply to the corresponding core-plus-look-ahead optimisation, not to a globally optimised annual problem. They do not bound the downstream effect of different committed decisions or certify an annual saving to the displayed rounding precision. Historical longer-limit diagnostic solves used the earlier tranche inputs and are not used to certify these corrected results. In particular, the event study's 1\% criterion must not be interpreted as a claim that all annual horizons meet that threshold.

The corrected central year-end checkpoint records 0.787115 CPU-hours outstanding at midnight and zero unserved work after the planned continuation. Its complete final look-ahead contains 2,531.359 kWh and GBP~98.275, including ordinary January demand. These quantities come from the current checkpoint supplied in \path{evidence/corrected_year_end_checkpoint.json}. Earlier terminal-value tests used different tranche inputs; their report is retained as historical context for the terminal convention, not as a terminal-sensitivity validation of the corrected central or enlarged-capacity cases.

For the event study, all 288 cells pass the recorded validation checks: 280 carry the boundary/cap flag and eight an unresolved-next-step flag. The 148 positive-duration dispatches meet the event solver-gap criterion of 1\% and the physical audits; the other 140 cells have no certified positive duration. Maximum target error is 0.1 kW, terminal-temperature error 0.05$^{\circ}$C, excess cohort residual $10^{-7}$ CPU-hours and component-sum residual approximately $4.82\times10^{-11}$ kW. An independent accounting check reconciles all positive-duration component traces against metered deviations. These checks establish consistency with the formulated constraints. They do not eliminate the search qualifications in S3, model approximation or uncertainty in the adopted facility parameters.
